JSON: Name: carmen_bbp_multiplex Title: Multiplexed CRISPR-Cas13 CARMEN assay pipeline for high-throughput detection of bloodborne pathogens Short Hypothesis: Incorporating deep-learning-designed crRNA assays into a CARMEN microfluidic CRISPR-Cas13 pipeline will produce lower or equal limits of detection and non-inferior specificity compared to standard RT-qPCR for multiplexed detection of 23 bloodborne pathogens in serum and clinical specimens. Related Work: RT-qPCR is the current diagnostic standard for single-target pathogen detection but has limited throughput, higher per-test cost at scale, and requires serial reactions for multiplexing. CRISPR-based diagnostics (Cas13/Cas12 SHERLOCK/DETECTR/SHINE) demonstrated sensitive, specific detection for individual targets and small panels, and have progressed toward field use, but they remain limited in multiplex capacity and clinical-scale validation. Microfluidic CARMEN has previously enabled massively multiplexed CRISPR-Cas13 detection across many sample-assay pairs, but prior implementations relied on larger instruments and had workflow complexity. Machine-learning guide-design approaches (e.g., ADAPT) can improve crRNA coverage across genomic diversity, yet systematic comparisons versus conventional guide selection in multiplexed, clinically relevant matrices are sparse. Remaining gaps include: (1) comprehensive evaluation of deep-learning-guided crRNAs in high-plex microfluidic CRISPR workflows; (2) head-to-head LOD and specificity comparisons against RT-qPCR across diverse pathogen classes and real clinical samples; and (3) assessment of platform transitions (older to newer microfluidic instruments) and extraction dependencies. Abstract: We address the need for scalable, multiplexed molecular diagnostics for bloodborne and febrile pathogens by developing and validating a CARMEN-based CRISPR-Cas13 pipeline that integrates deep-learning-guided crRNA design. The pipeline targets 23 clinically relevant pathogens across three panels (viral hemorrhagic fevers, mosquito-borne viruses, sexually transmitted infections) and adapts microfluidic detection to an updated instrument model to reduce workflow complexity. The approach combines automated guide design, pooled amplification, and microfluidic combinatorial CRISPR detection to enable simultaneous testing of many samples against many targets. The main contribution is a reproducible pipeline that quantifies analytical sensitivity (limit of detection), specificity, and concordance with RT-qPCR on synthetic material, contrived healthy serum, and confirmed-positive clinical specimens (including Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Lassa virus, and mpox). The expected outcome is an experimentally validated multiplex diagnostic workflow that demonstrates comparable or improved sensitivity relative to RT-qPCR while preserving specificity, enabling higher-throughput pathogen surveillance and diagnostic testing. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Synthetic nucleic acid targets: consensus DNA/RNA fragments representing each of the 23 target pathogen genomic loci, serially diluted from 1e5 to 1 copy/μL. (2) Contrived samples: pooled healthy normal serum (HNS) spiked with synthetic or extracted genomic RNA/DNA at concentrations 1e5–1 copies/μL. (3) Clinical cohorts: urine specimens for Neisseria gonorrhoeae (N=48; 10 RT-qPCR positives, 38 negatives), archived plasma/swab samples for Lassa virus (N=90 confirmed RT-qPCR positives) and mpox (N=42 confirmed RT-qPCR positives). Baselines: (A) Commercial/clinical RT-qPCR assays (site-standard kits per pathogen), (B) singleplex Cas13 assays using manually selected crRNAs, (C) multiplexed CARMEN with non-ADAPT guides. Metrics: analytical LOD (copies/μL via probit regression, 95% confidence), sensitivity/specificity, positive/negative percent agreement, ROC AUC, time-to-result, per-sample reagent cost, cross-reactivity rate, concordance of detection vs RT-qPCR Ct (Spearman rho and Bland-Altman). Experimental setup: (1) Guide design: run ADAPT to generate >=5 crRNA candidates per target; synthesize all. (2) Screening: test each crRNA candidate against 1e4 and 1e2 copies/μL of synthetic target in CARMEN; select top-performing guide(s) by median signal-to-NTC ratio (n=3 technical replicates). (3) LOD determination: test selected guides in pooled multiplexed CARMEN panels across serial dilutions with technical triplicates and 20 replicates at lowest concentrations; compute probit LOD. (4) Contrived HNS: spike-in at 1e5–1 copies/μL, extract nucleic acid (standardized kit), perform pooled amplification and BiomarkX CARMEN detection; run parallel RT-qPCR on same extracts. (5) Clinical validation: run CARMEN and RT-qPCR in parallel blind to prior results; analyze per-sample concordance; perform McNemar's test for paired sensitivity differences. Comparisons/Ablations: (i) ADAPT-designed guides vs manually designed guides (same pipeline); (ii) multiplexed CARMEN vs simplex Cas13 assays (same guides); (iii) BiomarkX detection vs BiomarkHD (instrument switch); (iv) assays with extraction vs assays on extraction-free protocol (if applicable). Statistical analyses: probit regression for LOD, McNemar test for paired diagnostic comparisons, ROC curves and AUC, Spearman correlation for fluorescence vs Ct, significance threshold p<0.05. Reproducibility: report technical and biological replicate counts, and provide raw signal distributions. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failures: guide cross-reactivity or tolerance of mismatches causing false positives/false negatives; variable amplification efficiency in pooled RT-PCR leading to target drop-out in high-plex pools; inconsistent reagent quality or Cas13 enzyme activity across lots. Data/evaluation biases: limited clinical sample diversity (geography, viral clades, specimen types); archived samples with variable degradation producing biased concordance; small sample sizes for some pathogens limiting statistical power. Scalability and compute: ADAPT deep-learning design requires compute resources and sequence databases for up-to-date coverage; microfluidic IFC throughput constrained by instrument availability and cost. Generalization limits: assay performance may decrease against divergent strains not represented in training genomes; reliance on nucleic acid extraction limits deployment in extraction-free low-resource settings. Regulatory and operational constraints: need for extensive clinical validation and quality-control standards before clinical deployment; cold-chain and supply dependencies for enzymes and reagents. Measurement limitations: LOD estimates depend on extraction efficiency and may not translate to real-world specimen variability; concordance with RT-qPCR may be impacted by differences in target regions and assay chemistry.
